question: Aqueous solutions may contain several kinds of positive and negative ions. Why might not every ion be discharged at its electrode during electrolysis?

title: Separating two causes of a colour change
question: Two identical cells contain blue copper(II) sulphate solution. Cell X uses copper electrodes; Cell Y uses graphite electrodes. Both are operated for the same period under comparable conditions. Which result is most consistent with their electrode reactions?

Cell X must produce hydrogen at the cathode while Cell Y produces copper.
Cell X cannot conduct because copper electrodes block ion movement.

title: Correcting a misconception about electrons
question: A student argues that because cations move towards the cathode, the cathode must supply positive ions to the electrolyte. Which explanation corrects the error?

options.text: Cations move towards the anode, not the cathode.
The cathode creates cations from neutral atoms without any reaction.
Cations move towards the cathode and gain electrons there; the cathode is the site of reduction.
Cations are discharged by losing electrons at the cathode.

explanation: Cations are attracted to the negative cathode, where they gain electrons. Their movement through the electrolyte and electron transfer at the electrode are distinct processes.

title: Final integrated challenge
question: A student carries out three experiments using inert electrodes: - **Experiment I:** Molten lead(II) bromide produces lead at one electrode and bromine at the other. - **Experiment II:** Aqueous copper(II) sulphate produces copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. - **Experiment III:** Acidified water produces hydrogen and oxygen in an approximate 2:1 volume ratio. Which statement correctly compares all three experiments?

options.text: Reduction occurs at the anode in all three experiments.
The anode is negative in all three experiments.
All three electrolytes produce hydrogen at the cathode.
Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode in all three experiments, although the products differ.

explanation:
The fundamental electrode processes remain the same: reduction at the cathode and oxidation at the anode. The actual products depend on the electrolyte and the conditions.
